title: Passover: clearing out
hookLine: the house is cleared of leaven; teachers call it clearing out puffed-up pride
tomorrow: Passover: a candle and a feather

cards: In the weeks before Passover, observant Jewish homes go a little wild. Couch cushions come off. Car seats get vacuumed for cereal.
Coat pockets are turned inside out for old cookies. The toaster gets put away, or given away. Kitchen cabinets are emptied and taped shut.
Someone finds a pretzel behind the fridge from two Passovers ago. It looks like spring cleaning, and in a way it is. But people aren't hunting for dust.
They're hunting for one thing, and the Torah gives it a name.

teach.b: The word is chametz: leaven, or anything that has risen. In Jewish law, chametz is grain from five kinds, wheat, barley, spelt, rye and oats, that has mixed with water and been left long enough to ferment.
Bread, pasta, cake, beer, cereal. The Torah is firm about it.

teach.h: PUT AWAY LEAVEN FROM YOUR HOUSES.
teach.b: In the old Jewish translation: "seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread; howbeit the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses." And not just don't eat it. Don't own it.
Don't let it be seen in your home. That's why the cleaning reaches the pockets and the car. Why leaven?
The plain answer is the story itself. Leaving Egypt, the Israelites had no time to let their dough rise, so they baked it flat. Matzah is the bread of hurry.
But the rabbis heard more in it.

In the Talmud, tractate Berakhot, a rabbi named Alexandri prays that God knows what really stops us from doing God's will: the yeast in the dough. The rabbis used that image for the inner pull toward wrong.
Later, Hasidic teachers made it personal. Chametz puffs up. It takes a little substance and fills it with air until it looks bigger than it is.
Matzah is just flour and water, flat, nothing added.
Another teaching points out that in Hebrew, chametz and matzah are spelled with almost the same letters; the difference is one small stroke.
So cleaning the house becomes cleaning the self: looking into the corners for anything swollen past its size.

how: In the weeks before Passover, observant Jews clean their homes, cars and workplaces of chametz, use separate Passover dishes, and formally sell or renounce any chametz they still own before the festival begins.

o: flat bread of flour and water, made in a hurry
leaven: grain that has risen, cleared for Passover

games.q: the Israelites are leaving Egypt tonight. the bread dough is mixed, but it hasn't risen. what do they do?
o: wait for the dough to rise.
bake it flat and take it with them.
games.why: they baked it as it was, unleavened: there wasn't time. matzah is the bread of hurry.

practice: If you can, clear one small spot now, a drawer, a bag, a car cup holder, while you breathe; if not, picture it.
Then look inward the same way for one place you've been puffed up lately, a story you've inflated, a credit that wasn't all yours, and let it shrink back to its real size.

wordCard.voice: Chametz. Leaven, grain that has risen: cleared out of the house before Passover, and for many teachers, a picture of pride. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: leaven, anything that has risen and fermented.

carryVoice: Your line: clear out the puffed-up. Plain flour and water, nothing added, is enough. Until tomorrow.
